latin.414: Deus vero cum peccatum hominibus imputat & vindictam exercet, Judicis partibus fungitur, nihilque habet ob oculos praeter justitiam, qua suum cuique tribuit. Itaque nulli alienum peccatum attribuit, nulli poenam irrogat ob peccatum, quod nec in se habuit, nec admisit: summa est justitiae eius puritas, summus nitor, & splendor. Octavo, Rex cum bellum denunciat vel infert, actu Rex est, & qua Rex caput subditorum, & ad subditos relationem actu habet, & vicissim subditi ad eum. Itaque, cum actu & plures sint, & se mutuis relationibus respiciant, actu unum corpus constituunt, ex Rege & subditis constans. Adamus vero cum peccavit actu pater non erat, actu relationem ad nos nullam habebat, non erat actu caput nostrum, & vicissim nos ad eum nullam relationem actu habebamus. Tum demum nata est haec relatio, cum pater esse, & liberos habere coepit. Est autem, postquam creatus fuerat, centum & triginta annis demum Seth natus, ex quo nos omnes sumus. Itaque qui nulli tum eramus, cum eo coire in societatem, aut componere corpus non potuimus. Subditi enim sunt actu, sunt actu subditi, actu Rex eorum est caput, actu eius imperata tenentur exequi, actu cum eo corpus componunt, actu eum vel consilio vel opibus, vel manu, vel saltem votis juvant. Deinde, an quia eramus in Adamo potentia, sequitur quod ille fecit nos fecisse, nobisque eius actiones imputari debere?
latin.415: Tu eras in eo potentia, an igitur fuisti vel actu, vel potentia maritus Evae primae parentis nostrae? An actu vel potentia genuisti Sethum secundum parentem generis humani? An in eo actu vel potentia resipuisti a peccato? Nempe illam unam actionem tu in eo fecisti, concupivisti scilicet fructum arboris vetitae, gustasti eius suavitatem, blanditiis & suasionibus uxoris tuae Evae te persuaderi sivisti, cupiditate sciendi bonum & malum flagrasti, divinitatem quandam affectasti, manum arbori prohibitae admovisti, fructum eius dentibus comminuisti. Equidem non capio cur istam unam actionem in Adamo ediderimus, a caeteris autem eius actionibus abstinuerimus. Alterum similitudinis membrum, seu, si ita mavis, similitudinem integram his verbis expressisti. Eodem modo si in urbe populus sit rebellis, & seditionem moveat in principis ministros, vel satellites, & eam ob causam princeps populum illum rebellionis damnet, & armis persequatur, seditio illa non tantum eorum esse censetur, qui se commoverunt primi, & injuriam fecerunt satellitibus, sed etiam imputatur coetui & toti communitati, seu societati civium. Omnes habentur rei rebelles, bona proscribuntur, nec parcitur vitae; quia sunt ex corpore, & societate illius urbis rebellis. Sic se res habet in genere humano. Primus homo tanquam caput omnium hominum, rebellans Deo & peccans in Deum, justo Dei judicio punitus est; non tantum ipse in persona sua, sed tota natura humana & omnes homines, qui sunt tanquam unum corpus, & coeunt in unam societatem; Et haec rebellio capitis, quae totam naturam pervasit, tribuitur & imputatur omnibus hominibus.
latin.416: Quae ad praecedentem similitudinem dicta sunt hanc ipsam quoque evertunt. Addam tamen pauca. Modo Adamum comparabas Regi bellum inferenti: Nunc eundem comparas populo rebellanti adversus Regis ministros. At quid habet Adamus commune cum seditiosa & tumultuante plebe alicuius urbis, in societatem rebellionis ipsos suos magistratus trahente, nisi eam coerceant pro virili, & se Regi purgent? Hinc facilius concludas multitudinis hominum peccata ipsi Adamo, quam unius Adami primum peccatum actuale toti hominum multitudini imputari debere. Deinde, putasne justum & aequum Regem id crimen illud rebellionis imputare, quos pro comperto habet in rebellionem non consensisse in illa urbe? Discernit proculdubio pro sua aequitate inter rebelles & non rebelles, seditiosos & in officio constantes. Praeterea, annon inde sequeretur multo propius & certius, multitudinis impiae peccata imputari paucis inter improbos delitescentibus piis, quam unius hominis peccatum unum, nullo alio homine praesente, immo existente, commissum omnibus hominibus imputari? Attamen ab illa imputatione Dei justitia abhorret. Absit tibi, dicebat Abraham Gen. 18. 25. Ut facias tale quidpiam, morti tradendo justum cum injusto, ut ita sit justo sicut injusto: Absit tibi; An judex totius terrae non exerceret jus? Vides quantopere pater credentium pugnare cum divina justitia credebat, si paucissimi justi magnae civitatis rebellis & peccatricis punitione cum civium multitudine involverentur, & nos eius filii audebimus Deo eiusmodi justitiam tribuere, quae unius hominis culpam imputet omnibus, non modo ad mortem aeternam, sed etiam ad eam poenam quae sit ipsa proprie malum culpae, & causa omnium peccatorum? Absit, absit a nobis talis, de Deo nostro, de mundi judice, cuius aequitas & justitia nobis notissima est, cogitatio!
latin.417: GAR. Mittamus nunc quidem Rhetoricationes, & quod de poena dicitur, quae sit ipsa specie malum culpae, quia de hoc & aliquid dictum est superius, & recurret postea ea de re fusius disputandi occasio. Argumenti duntaxat vim attendamus, quod ita pertexi potest. Justos cum injustis eadem condemnatione & morte involvi, alienum est a Dei justitia, teste Abrahamo. Atqui in alieni peccati imputatione, justi cum injustis, eadem condemnatione & morte involverentur. Ergo alieni peccati imputatio est a Dei justitia aliena. PLAC. Qua occasione, & quam apposite testimonium Abrahami fuerit a me allatum Lector prudens, si placet, considerabit. Interim Argumentum quod hic vir doctus contexuit libenter pro meo habebo, modo in minore alieni peccati imputatio, non quaelibet intelligatur, sed ea duntaxat, de qua inter nos lis est, nempe antecedens omne peccatum nobis inhaerens aut a nobis commissum.
latin.418: GAR. Hic primum responderi posset, qua ab Abrahamo causa disceptatur, eam a Quaestione imputatae Adami inobedientiae longe abesse. Abrahamus enim de iis loquitur, qui non omnes eadem conditione agebant, sed alii justi erant, alii injustitiae mancipati: & quorum ea erat ratio, ut non modo justi propter impios, quibus commixti erant, in earundem poenarum consortium trahi possent, sed etiam impii propter justos eiusdem beneficii & conservationis esse participes; Unde Abrahamus utrumque a Deo precibus contendit, tum ut ne justi propter impiorum scelera pereant, tum ut impiis propter justos ignoscatur. Atqui longe aliter res habet in nostro negotio. Nam primo inter eos quibus Adae peccatum imputatur, hoc quidem respectu, nulla est justitiae injustitiaeve distinctio; neque enim solus Adamus injustus est, posteri vero justi & innocentes, sed omnes naturae seminis corruptione polluti, sicut explicatum est cap. 2. Deinde nec quinquaginta, nec viginti, nec decem, ac ne unus quidem est in hoc ordine carnaliter generatorum, propter cuius justitiam Deus caeteris parcere aut velit, aut debeat. Itaque ex Abrahami verbis duci non potest legitima adversus imputationem peccati Adae consequentia. PLAC. Horum duorum discriminum prius quidem appositum est, si de imputatione mediata agitur, quae supponit & consequitur inhaerentem corruptionem seu injustitiam.
latin.419: Ideo enim eadem condemnatione & morte cum injusto Adamo involvimur, quoniam & ipsi in nobis ipsis injusti sumus: sed si de imputatione immediata, quam solam impugno, agitur, falsum est; antecedit enim imputatio corruptionem haereditariam ut culpae poenam. Itaque nostra injustitia huiusmodi imputationem & condemnationem sequitur ut effectum, non antecedit ut causa. Non ideo eadem cum injusto Adamo condemnatione involvimur, quia sumus injusti, sed contra ideo sumus injusti, quia eadem cum injusto Adamo condemnatione involvimur: ita enim sumus imputatione peccati actualis ab Adamo commissi peccatores, id est, rei, & ut puniatur imputatum nobis illud peccatum sumus inhaerenter injusti. Sepósita igitur hac imputatione seu condemnatione nocens est Adamus, nos innocentes. Quare illa imputatio seu condemnatio, judice Abrahamo, pugnat cum Dei justitia. Posterius discrimen quid ad rem faciat, de qua agitur, non video.

pass_a.414: Placeus completes the seventh: God as Judge looks only to justice that gives each his due—attributes no alien sin, penalizes no one for a sin not his; highest purity of justice. Eighth: a King at war is actually King and head, actually related to subjects who with him actually make one body. Adam when he sinned was not actually father or head, had no actual relation to us—that relation began only when he became a father; Seth came only after 130 years. We who then were nothing could not compose a body with him as subjects actually do. Does potential presence in Adam mean we did what he did and his acts must be imputed to us?
pass_a.415: Potentiality absurdities pressed: if you were in Adam potentially, were you then actually or potentially Eve's husband, Seth's begetter, one who repented? Did you alone among his acts covet the forbidden fruit, taste it, yield to Eve's blandishments, burn to know good and evil, affect divinity, put hand to the tree and crush the fruit with teeth? Why that one action in Adam and abstinence from the rest? Opponent then states the second member: a rebellious city—sedition is imputed not only to first movers but to the whole community; all held rebels because of the body. So the first man as head rebelling against God is punished not only in his person but all human nature and all men as one body and society; the head's rebellion that pervaded nature is attributed and imputed to all.
pass_a.416: What overturned the King-war likeness overturns this too. The opponent shifted figures: Adam was a King making war, now rebellious commons drawing magistrates into sedition—Adam has little in common with that tumult; from it one would more easily impute the multitude's sins to Adam than one Adam actual-sin to all. A just King would not charge known non-consenters; he discerns rebels from those constant in duty. Still nearer: the impious multitude's sins on a few pious lurking among the wicked than one lone man's sin on all—yet God's justice abhors that. Abraham Gen. 18:25: far be it to deliver the just with the unjust; shall the Judge of all the earth not do right? If the fewest just must not share a great rebellious city's doom, dare we attribute to God a justice that imputes one man's fault to all—not only unto eternal death but unto that penalty which is itself the evil of fault and cause of all sins? Far, far from us such a thought of our God.
pass_a.417: GAR sets aside rhetoric about a penalty that is itself the evil of fault (treated above; more later) and weaves the syllogism: involving the just with the unjust in the same condemnation and death is alien to God's justice, Abraham witnessing; but in another's-sin imputation the just would be so involved; therefore another's-sin imputation is alien to God's justice. Placeus: the prudent Reader may weigh how aptly Abraham was brought; he gladly takes the argument as his own if the minor understands only the imputation in dispute between them—namely that which precedes every sin inhering in us or committed by us.
pass_a.418: GAR answers that Abraham's cause is far from the Question of Adam's imputed disobedience. Abraham spoke of mixed just and unjust, praying both that the just not perish for the impious and that the impious be spared for the just. Here, among those to whom Adam's sin is imputed, there is no such justice/injustice split: not Adam alone unjust and posterity innocent, but all polluted by seed-corruption (cap. 2); and there is no fifty or twenty or ten or even one carnal-born for whose justice God would or ought to spare the rest. So no legitimate consequence against imputation follows from Abraham. Placeus: of the two discriminations the former is apt if mediate imputation is meant—which presupposes and follows inhering corruption or injustice.
pass_a.419: Under that mediate reading we share unjust Adam's condemnation because we ourselves are unjust; but if immediate imputation—which alone Placeus fights—is meant, that is false: the imputation precedes hereditary corruption as the fault's penalty, so our injustice follows as effect and does not precede as cause. We are not condemned with Adam because we are unjust; rather we are unjust because condemned with him—by imputation of his actual sin made guilty, and made inherently unjust so that imputed sin may be punished. Set the imputation aside: Adam is the guilty one, we innocents. Therefore that imputation or condemnation, Abraham judging, clashes with God's justice. What the second discrimination does for the matter, Placeus does not see. Tip before GAR's further answer from Ezek 21.

414: But God, when he imputes sin to men and exercises vengeance, plays a Judge's part, and has nothing before his eyes but justice, which gives each his due. So he attributes no alien sin to anyone, nor lays a penalty on anyone for a sin he neither had in himself nor committed: the purity of his justice is highest, its brightness and splendor highest. Eighth: when a King declares or makes war, he is actually King, and as King head of subjects, and actually has relation to subjects, and they to him. So when they actually are many and regard one another by mutual relations, they actually constitute one body consisting of King and subjects. But Adam, when he sinned, was not actually father, actually had no relation to us, was not actually our head, and we actually had no relation to him. That relation was born only when he began to be a father and have children. And after he was created, only at a hundred and thirty years was Seth born, from whom we all are. So we who then were nothing could not join society with him or compose a body. Subjects actually are subjects; actually their King is head; actually they are bound to execute his commands; actually they compose a body with him; actually they help him by counsel or wealth or hand or at least by vows. Next: because we were in Adam potentially, does it follow that what he did we did, and that his actions ought to be imputed to us?
415: You were in him potentially—were you then actually or potentially husband of Eve our first parent? Did you actually or potentially beget Seth, second parent of the human race? Did you in him actually or potentially repent of sin? Namely you did that one action in him: you coveted the fruit of the forbidden tree, tasted its sweetness, let yourself be persuaded by Eve your wife's blandishments and suasions, burned with desire to know good and evil, affected a kind of divinity, put your hand to the forbidden tree, crushed its fruit with your teeth. I for my part do not grasp why we should have performed that one action in Adam and yet abstained from his other actions. You expressed the other member of the likeness—or, if you prefer, a whole likeness—in these words. In the same way if in a city the people are rebellious and raise sedition against the prince's ministers or satellites, and for that cause the prince condemns that people of rebellion and pursues them with arms, that sedition is judged not only theirs who first stirred and injured the satellites, but is also imputed to the assembly and whole community or society of citizens. All are held guilty rebels, goods are proscribed, nor is life spared; because they are of the body and society of that rebellious city. So it stands with the human race. The first man as head of all men, rebelling against God and sinning against God, was punished by God's just judgment; not only himself in his person, but all human nature and all men, who are as one body and gather into one society; And this rebellion of the head, which pervaded all nature, is attributed and imputed to all men.
416: What was said against the preceding likeness overturns this one too. Yet I will add a few things. Just now you compared Adam to a King making war: now you compare the same man to a people rebelling against the King's ministers. But what has Adam in common with the seditious and tumultuous commons of some city, drawing even their own magistrates into the society of rebellion unless they curb it with all their might and clear themselves to the King? From this you would more easily conclude that the multitude's sins ought to be imputed to Adam himself than that one Adam's first actual sin ought to be imputed to the whole multitude of men. Next, do you think a just and equitable King would impute that crime of rebellion to those he knows for certain did not consent to the rebellion in that city? He doubtless discerns by his equity between rebels and non-rebels, the seditious and those constant in duty. Further, would it not follow much more nearly and surely that the sins of an impious multitude are imputed to a few pious men lurking among the wicked, than that one sin of one man, committed with no other man present—indeed existing—is imputed to all men? Yet God's justice abhors that imputation. Far be it from you, said Abraham Gen. 18:25, to do such a thing, delivering the just to death with the unjust, so that it be with the just as with the unjust: Far be it from you; shall the Judge of all the earth not do right? You see how strongly the father of believers thought it would clash with divine justice if the fewest just of a great rebellious and sinning city were involved in punishment with the multitude of citizens—and shall we his sons dare attribute to God a justice that imputes one man's fault to all, not only unto eternal death, but even unto that penalty which is itself properly the evil of fault and the cause of all sins? Far, far from us such a thought of our God, the world's Judge, whose equity and justice are most known to us!
417: GAR. Let us now drop the rhetorics, and what is said of a penalty that is itself in kind the evil of fault—something was said of this above, and occasion will return later to dispute it more fully. Let us attend only to the force of the argument, which can be woven thus. That the just be involved with the unjust in the same condemnation and death is alien to God's justice, Abraham witnessing. But in the imputation of another's sin, the just would be involved with the unjust in the same condemnation and death. Therefore the imputation of another's sin is alien to God's justice. PLAC. On what occasion, and how aptly, Abraham's testimony was brought by me the prudent Reader will consider if he please. Meanwhile the Argument the learned man has woven here I gladly take as my own, provided that in the minor "imputation of another's sin" is not understood of any whatever, but only of that about which the dispute between us is—namely that which precedes every sin inhering in us or committed by us.
418: GAR. Here it could first be answered that the cause Abraham debates is far from the Question of Adam's imputed disobedience. For Abraham speaks of those who were not all in the same condition, but some were just, others enslaved to injustice: and whose ratio was such that not only could the just be drawn into partnership of the same penalties for the impious with whom they were mixed, but also the impious could share the same benefit and preservation for the just; Whence Abraham pressed God with prayers for both—that the just not perish for the impious' crimes, and that the impious be pardoned for the just. Yet our business stands far otherwise. For first among those to whom Adam's sin is imputed, in this respect there is no distinction of justice or injustice; for not Adam alone is unjust and posterity just and innocent, but all are polluted by corruption of the seed's nature, as was explained in cap. 2. Next there are neither fifty nor twenty nor ten nor even one in this order of those carnally generated for whose justice God would or ought to spare the rest. So from Abraham's words no legitimate consequence against imputation of Adam's sin can be drawn. PLAC. Of these two discriminations the former is indeed apt if mediate imputation is in view, which presupposes and follows inhering corruption or injustice.
419: For that is why we are involved in the same condemnation and death with unjust Adam—because we ourselves are unjust in ourselves: but if immediate imputation, which alone I impugn, is in view, that is false; for the imputation precedes hereditary corruption as the penalty of the fault. So our injustice follows this kind of imputation and condemnation as effect, and does not precede as cause. We are not involved in the same condemnation with unjust Adam because we are unjust, but on the contrary we are unjust because we are involved in the same condemnation with unjust Adam: for so by imputation of the actual sin Adam committed we are made sinners—that is, guilty—and that that imputed sin may be punished we are made inherently unjust. Set aside this imputation or condemnation and Adam is the guilty one, we innocents. Therefore that imputation or condemnation, Abraham judging, clashes with God's justice. What the latter discrimination does for the matter at hand, I do not see.
